error_modes.label: Distance from the arc (DME) during the intercept

texts.0: SP, due to a late and shallow turn onto the arc with no correction turns applied to the raw DME trend, did not stop the aircraft on the published DME arc. The distance from the arc exceeded 2 DME and kept increasing outside the arc with no turn back toward it. IP had to intervene and direct the correcting turn to regain the published DME arc.
texts.1: SP, due to reading the DME window without following its rate of change, did not apply timely correction turns to regain the arc. The distance from the arc reached 2 DME, at the tolerance limit, and SP turned back only after repeated verbal instruction from IP. The arc was eventually regained, but the deviation persisted through most of the intercept.
texts.2: SP, due to a slightly late roll-in on the intercept turn, did not roll out exactly on the published arc distance. The aircraft settled about 1.5 DME outside the arc, between the 1 DME and 2 DME limits. SP identified the trend on the DME readout and turned back to the arc in time, without verbal prompting or IP intervention.
texts.3: SP rolled out on the published DME arc and maintained the distance from the arc within 1 DME throughout the intercept. Corrections were made early and in small turn increments, so the DME readout was stabilized promptly on the nominal distance.
texts.4: SP flew the arc intercept with the distance from the arc never exceeding about 0.3 DME. The roll-out was placed on the arc with correctly anticipated lead, and the DME readout stayed essentially constant, requiring only minimal turn corrections.
texts.marginal: SP kept the distance from the arc inside the required tolerance, but the readout consistently rode near 0.9-1.0 DME outside the arc instead of being centered on it. Corrections were initiated late and in large increments, so the same drift toward the tolerance limit repeated on each intercept. SP is expected to anticipate the drift earlier and use smaller, earlier turns to hold the arc closer to the nominal distance.

texts_at.0: SP flew the arc intercept with the IP flying the first correction turns and talking through the DME trend as the exercise began. This is SP's first exposure to reading the DME window as a rate rather than a static distance, and applying timely correction turns from it has not yet been built. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to begin reading the DME trend independently, with the IP available to confirm the picture.
texts_at.1: SP flew the arc intercept to the standard expected at this stage, letting the distance from the arc reach 2 DME, at the tolerance limit, before the turn back was made. The correction followed repeated verbal instruction from IP rather than SP's own read of the DME trend. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to follow the rate of change on the DME window rather than reading it as a static value.
texts_at.2: SP identified the trend on the DME readout without prompting on the intercept, settling about 1.5 DME outside the arc before turning back to the arc in time. The correction turn is still made in one step rather than several smaller ones as the technique favors. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to use smaller, earlier turn increments so the settling distance moves closer to the nominal arc.
texts_at.3: SP rolled out on the published DME arc and maintained the distance from the arc within 1 DME through most of the intercept, with corrections made early and in small increments. One correction ran slightly wide before being brought back in, without the arc distance leaving the standard. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to make that correction as promptly as the others so the DME readout stabilizes without the wider excursion.

texts_above.1: SP flew the arc intercept, holding the distance from the arc to about 2 DME, at the tolerance limit, before the turn back regained the arc. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP identified the trend on the DME readout without prompting on the intercept, settling about 1.5 DME outside the arc before turning back to the arc in time. Using smaller, earlier turn increments, rather than one larger correction, would bring that settling distance closer to nominal. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound arc-tracking technique.
texts_above.3: SP rolled out on the published DME arc and maintained the distance from the arc within 1 DME throughout the intercept, with corrections made early and in small turn increments that stabilized the DME readout promptly on the nominal distance. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good lead-point application.
texts_above.4: SP flew the arc intercept with the distance from the arc never exceeding about 0.3 DME, with the roll-out placed on the arc through correctly anticipated lead and the DME readout staying essentially constant. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding arc-distance control.

error_modes.label: Lead computation and turn onto the arc
error_modes.source: general:null (Basic A/C Control Criteria apply) | conditions:same as Course Intercepts | xref:instrument-12:a,b

texts.0: SP, due to lack of knowledge of the standard lead used to turn onto a DME arc, did not solve the intercept problem according to standardized procedures. SP started the turn abeam the arc with no lead applied, and the aircraft cut inside the arc by more than 2 DME. IP had to intervene and take over the correcting turn to place the aircraft back on the published arc.
texts.1: SP, due to lack of knowledge of the relationship between groundspeed, bank angle and lead distance, did not compute a usable lead point for the turn onto the arc. The turn was started late and the aircraft rolled out about 2 DME outside the arc, at the tolerance limit, and was brought back only after IP verbally directed the correction. The intercept was completed, but the geometry was never re-established by SP alone.
texts.2: SP, due to an approximate rather than computed lead for the turn onto the arc, did not roll out on the published DME distance. The aircraft passed about 1.5 DME inside the arc, between the 1 DME and 2 DME limits, before the trend was arrested. SP recognized the error from the DME readout and corrected back onto the arc without any IP input.
texts.3: SP computed the lead for the turn onto the arc according to standardized procedures and rolled out on the published DME distance within 1 DME. The bank angle chosen matched the groundspeed, so the roll-out required no additional correction turn.
texts.4: SP applied the correct lead for the turn onto the arc and rolled out on the published distance with a deviation of no more than about 0.3 DME. The intercept geometry was solved before the turn was started, so the arc was captured in a single continuous turn with no re-intercept required.
texts.marginal: SP applied a lead for the turn onto the arc and stayed inside the required tolerance, but the lead used was the same for every intercept regardless of groundspeed. Each roll-out therefore finished around 0.9 DME off the published distance and required an additional correction turn. SP is expected to adjust the lead to the actual groundspeed and bank so that the arc is captured without a follow-up correction.

texts_at.0: SP turned onto the arc with the IP computing the lead point and talking through the relationship between groundspeed, bank angle and lead distance. This is SP's first exposure to computing a lead point for a DME arc, and relating groundspeed and bank to the lead distance has not yet been learned well enough to apply without help. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to begin computing the lead point independently from groundspeed and bank, with the IP available to confirm the figure.
texts_at.1: SP computed a lead for the turn onto the arc to the standard expected at this stage, rolling out about 2 DME outside the arc, at the tolerance limit, before the correction closed the geometry. The correction followed IP's verbal direction rather than SP's own recomputation. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to relate groundspeed and bank angle to the lead distance directly rather than approximating it.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the error from the DME readout without prompting, passing about 1.5 DME inside the arc before correcting back onto the arc unaided. The lead used is still approximate rather than computed for the groundspeed and bank actually flown. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to compute the lead from groundspeed and bank before the turn rather than estimating it.
texts_at.3: SP computed the lead for the turn onto the arc according to standardized procedures and rolled out on the published DME distance within 1 DME on most intercepts. One intercept needed a small additional correction turn after a slightly early roll-in, without the arc distance leaving the standard. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to time that roll-in as precisely as on the other intercepts.

texts_above.1: SP computed a lead for the turn onto the arc, rolling out about 2 DME outside the arc, at the tolerance limit, before the correction closed the geometry. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the error from the DME readout without prompting, passing about 1.5 DME inside the arc before correcting back onto the arc unaided. Computing the lead from groundspeed and bank before the turn, rather than estimating it, would remove that pass-through. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid lead computation.
texts_above.3: SP computed the lead for the turn onto the arc according to standardized procedures and rolled out on the published DME distance within 1 DME, with the bank angle chosen matching the groundspeed so the roll-out required no additional correction turn. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed intercept planning.
texts_above.4: SP applied the correct lead for the turn onto the arc and rolled out on the published distance with a deviation of no more than about 0.3 DME, solving the intercept geometry before the turn was started so the arc was captured in a single continuous turn. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional geometry judgment.

error_modes.label: Altitude control while intercepting and holding the arc
error_modes.source: general:null (Basic A/C Control Criteria apply) | xref:instrument-04:ALTITUDE (feet)

texts.0: SP, due to attention concentrated on the DME readout during the turn onto the arc, did not maintain the assigned altitude. Back pressure was not added as bank was applied and the aircraft descended more than 300 feet below the assigned altitude with an increasing rate. IP had to intervene and initiate the recovery to the assigned altitude.
texts.1: SP, due to failure to trim after the roll-in on the arc intercept, did not hold the assigned altitude. The aircraft reached 300 feet off the assigned altitude, at the tolerance limit, and SP started the correction only after IP verbally called the deviation. The altitude was regained slowly and the same trend reappeared during the arc.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed power adjustment when bank was increased for the intercept turn, did not hold the assigned altitude precisely. The aircraft deviated about 200 feet, between the 150 foot and 300 foot limits, before the trend was arrested. SP detected the deviation on the altimeter and returned to the assigned altitude in time without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP maintained the assigned altitude within 150 feet throughout the turn onto the arc and along the arc. Pitch and power were coordinated with the bank changes, so altitude excursions were arrested as soon as they appeared.
texts.4: SP held the assigned altitude with deviations of no more than about 40 feet during the whole arc intercept. Altitude was protected during every turn onto and off the arc, with the altimeter needle remaining essentially stationary.
texts.marginal: SP remained within the altitude tolerance, but the aircraft was consistently 130-150 feet low every time bank was applied for a correction turn on the arc. The deviation was corrected each time, yet it recurred with the same pattern on each turn. SP is expected to anticipate the pitch requirement with bank so that altitude is held closer to the assigned value.

texts_at.0: SP flew the turn onto and along the arc with the IP calling the altitude trend and talking through the trim needed as bank was applied. This is SP's first exposure to holding altitude through the turn onto a DME arc, and trimming immediately after the roll-in has not yet been built. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to begin trimming independently after the roll-in, with the IP available to call any trend that develops.
texts_at.1: SP held altitude while intercepting the arc to the standard expected at this stage, reaching 300 feet off the assigned altitude, at the tolerance limit, before the correction was made. The correction followed IP's verbal call rather than SP's own trim discipline after the roll-in. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to trim immediately after the roll-in on the arc intercept rather than holding the aircraft with continuous back pressure.
texts_at.2: SP detected the deviation on the altimeter without prompting on the intercept, letting it reach about 200 feet before returning to the assigned altitude in time. The power adjustment for the increased bank is still made a moment after the turn is started rather than with it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to add the power adjustment together with the bank input rather than after the turn is under way.
texts_at.3: SP maintained the assigned altitude within 150 feet throughout the turn onto the arc and along the arc on most intercepts, coordinating pitch and power with the bank changes. One intercept showed a slightly larger excursion during a steeper turn, arrested as soon as it appeared without a change in technique. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to hold the same coordination at the steeper bank angles as at the shallower ones.

texts_above.1: SP held altitude while intercepting the arc, containing the deviation to about 300 feet, at the tolerance limit, before the correction was made. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP detected the deviation on the altimeter without prompting on the intercept, reaching about 200 feet before returning to the assigned altitude in time. Adding the power adjustment together with the bank input, rather than after the turn is under way, would keep that excursion smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady altitude discipline.
texts_above.3: SP maintained the assigned altitude within 150 feet throughout the turn onto the arc and along the arc, coordinating pitch and power with the bank changes so altitude excursions were arrested as soon as they appeared. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed pitch-and-bank coordination.
texts_above.4: SP held the assigned altitude with deviations of no more than about 40 feet during the whole arc intercept, protecting altitude during every turn onto and off the arc with the altimeter needle remaining essentially stationary. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior altitude anticipation.

error_modes.label: Airspeed control during the arc intercept
error_modes.source: general:null (Basic A/C Control Criteria apply) | xref:instrument-04:AIRSPEED (KIAS)

texts.0: SP, due to leaving the power lever unattended while working the navigation problem, did not control the engine power for the phase of flight. Airspeed decayed more than 20 KIAS below the briefed value and continued to reduce while the correcting turn was flown. IP had to intervene and restore power to recover the briefed airspeed.
texts.1: SP, due to a large unchecked power reduction during the turn onto the arc, did not maintain the briefed airspeed. Airspeed reached 20 KIAS off the briefed value, at the tolerance limit, and was corrected only after IP called for a power change. The airspeed then oscillated as power was applied in large steps.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed power increase when bank was applied for the arc intercept, did not hold the briefed airspeed precisely. Airspeed deviated about 15 KIAS, between the 10 KIAS and 20 KIAS limits, before the trend was reversed. SP saw the trend on the airspeed indicator and reset power in time, without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP controlled engine power according to the phase of flight and maintained the briefed airspeed within 10 KIAS during the intercept and along the arc. Power adjustments were made in small increments as bank was applied and removed.
texts.4: SP maintained the briefed airspeed with deviations of no more than about 4 KIAS throughout the arc intercept. Power was adjusted proactively with each bank change, so the airspeed indication stayed practically constant.
texts.marginal: SP stayed within the airspeed tolerance, but the aircraft was carried about 9 KIAS fast for most of the arc, which increased the required lead and made every correction turn wider. Power was reset only after the deviation had developed rather than with the bank change. SP is expected to set power together with the turn so that the briefed airspeed is held closer to the target value.

texts_at.0: SP flew the arc intercept with the IP calling the airspeed trend and talking through the power changes needed as bank was applied. This is SP's first exposure to controlling power through the turn onto a DME arc, and checking the airspeed indicator with the bank change has not yet become routine. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to begin adjusting power independently with the bank change, with the IP available to call any trend that develops.
texts_at.1: SP held airspeed during the arc intercept to the standard expected at this stage, reaching 20 KIAS off the briefed value, at the tolerance limit, before the correction was made. The correction followed IP calling for a power change rather than SP's own read of the airspeed trend. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to bring the airspeed indicator into the scan with the bank change rather than after the deviation has become established.
texts_at.2: SP saw the trend on the airspeed indicator without prompting during the intercept, with the error reaching about 15 KIAS before resetting power in time. The power increase for the bank change is still applied a moment after the turn is started rather than with it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to add power together with the bank input rather than reacting to the airspeed once it has already moved.
texts_at.3: SP controlled engine power according to the phase of flight and maintained the briefed airspeed within 10 KIAS during the intercept and along the arc on most turns, with adjustments made in small increments as bank was applied and removed. One turn needed a slightly larger correction following a steeper bank angle, without leaving the standard. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to size that adjustment as finely as on the other turns.

texts_above.1: SP held airspeed during the arc intercept, containing the deviation to about 20 KIAS, at the tolerance limit, before the correction was made. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP saw the trend on the airspeed indicator without prompting during the intercept, reaching about 15 KIAS before resetting power in time. Adding power together with the bank input, rather than reacting once the airspeed has moved, would keep that trend smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable power anticipation.
texts_above.3: SP controlled engine power according to the phase of flight and maintained the briefed airspeed within 10 KIAS during the intercept and along the arc, with adjustments made in small increments as bank was applied and removed. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good power management.
texts_above.4: SP maintained the briefed airspeed with deviations of no more than about 4 KIAS throughout the arc intercept, adjusting power proactively with each bank change so the airspeed indication stayed practically constant. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional airspeed anticipation.

error_modes.label: Heading and bank discipline on correction turns
error_modes.source: general:null (Basic A/C Control Criteria apply) | xref:instrument-04:HEADING (degrees), instrument-04:execution (bank up to 30 degrees)

texts.0: SP, due to chasing the DME readout with continuous uncoordinated turns, did not fly controlled correction headings on the arc. Bank was increased past 30 degrees and the rollout heading was missed by more than 10 degrees, so the aircraft never settled on a stable arc heading. IP had to intervene and take the aircraft back to a controlled heading on the arc.
texts.1: SP, due to rolling out without reference to a computed arc heading, did not stop the turns on the required headings. The rollout heading was off by 10 degrees, at the tolerance limit, and was corrected only after IP verbally provided the heading to fly. Successive corrections repeated the same overshoot pattern.
texts.2: SP, due to a slightly high roll-out rate on the correction turn, did not stop exactly on the required arc heading. The rollout heading was off by about 8 degrees, between the 5 degree and 10 degree limits. SP identified the overshoot on the HSI and corrected back to the required heading promptly without IP input.
texts.3: SP used bank within 30 degrees for all correction turns and rolled out on the required arc headings within 5 degrees. Turns were coordinated and each heading was held until the next correction was required by the DME trend.
texts.4: SP flew all correction turns on the arc with smooth, coordinated bank and rolled out on the required headings within about 2 degrees. Turn increments were sized to the DME trend, so no heading overshoot or reversal was needed.
texts.marginal: SP held rollout headings inside the tolerance, but each correction turn finished about 4-5 degrees past the required heading and had to be nudged back. The bank used was larger than needed for the small DME corrections required. SP is expected to size the correction turns to the actual deviation and anticipate the roll-out so that headings are captured directly.

texts_at.0: SP flew correction turns on the arc with the IP calling the required heading and talking through the bank used for each turn. This is SP's first exposure to stopping a correction turn on a computed arc heading, and judging the roll-out rate for it has not yet been built. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to begin computing an arc heading independently before each correction turn, with the IP available to confirm the roll-out.
texts_at.1: SP flew correction turns on the arc to the standard expected at this stage, missing the required heading by 10 degrees, at the tolerance limit, before it was corrected. The correction followed IP verbally providing the heading rather than SP's own reference. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to compute an arc heading before each correction turn rather than rolling out without a target.
texts_at.2: SP identified the overshoot on the HSI without prompting on the correction turns, missing the required heading by about 8 degrees before correcting back promptly. The roll-out rate on that turn is still slightly high for the heading required. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to reduce the roll-out rate as the target heading is approached rather than after it has been passed.
texts_at.3: SP used bank within 30 degrees for all correction turns and rolled out on the required arc headings within 5 degrees on most turns, holding each heading until the next correction was required by the DME trend. One turn needed a small nudge after a slightly wide roll-out, without a change in the bank discipline used. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to roll out on that turn as precisely as on the others.

texts_above.1: SP flew correction turns on the arc, missing the required heading by about 10 degrees, at the tolerance limit, before it was corrected. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP identified the overshoot on the HSI without prompting on the correction turns, missing the required heading by about 8 degrees before correcting back promptly. Reducing the roll-out rate as the target heading is approached, rather than after passing it, would remove that overshoot. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured heading discipline.
texts_above.3: SP used bank within 30 degrees for all correction turns and rolled out on the required arc headings within 5 degrees, holding each heading until the next correction was required by the DME trend and keeping the turns coordinated throughout. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise bank-and-heading control.
texts_above.4: SP flew all correction turns on the arc with smooth, coordinated bank and rolled out on the required headings within about 2 degrees, sizing turn increments to the DME trend so no heading overshoot or reversal was needed. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate turn discipline.

error_modes.label: Navigation aid setup and instrument cross-check
error_modes.source: general:null (Basic A/C Control Criteria apply) | xref:instrument-04:d

texts.0: SP, due to an interrupted instrument cross-check while attention stayed on a single navigation display, did not use the radio aids to maintain orientation on the arc. The station and the correct navigation source were not verified, so SP flew an intercept against an unchecked indication and ended more than 2 DME off the published arc while unaware of the aircraft position. IP had to intervene, identify the correct source and re-establish the aircraft on the arc.
texts.1: SP, due to absent cross-check of aircraft state against the primary flight instruments, did not confirm the navigation setup before starting the arc intercept. The error was recognized only after IP verbally directed a check of the navigation source, by which time the distance from the arc was 2 DME, at the tolerance limit. Orientation was restored, but only with continuous verbal guidance.
texts.2: SP, due to a cross-check that dwelt too long on the DME readout, did not scan the bearing pointer and the flight instruments at the same rate. The delayed information caused the aircraft to drift about 1.5 DME off the arc, between the 1 DME and 2 DME limits. SP resumed a full cross-check on its own initiative and corrected back onto the arc without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP verified the navigation aid setup before the intercept and maintained a continuous cross-check between the bearing pointer, the DME readout and the flight instruments. Orientation relative to the station was maintained at all times and the arc was held within 1 DME.
texts.4: SP checked and identified the navigation source before the intercept and kept an even, uninterrupted cross-check throughout the arc. Aircraft position relative to the station was reported accurately at any moment and the arc was held within about 0.3 DME.
texts.marginal: SP kept the aircraft on the arc within the required tolerance, but the cross-check remained weighted toward the DME readout, with the flight instruments scanned only after a deviation had built. The navigation setup was verified once and not re-checked after the source was changed. SP is expected to keep an even scan rate across the navigation and flight instruments so that deviations are seen as they start.

texts_at.0: SP held orientation on the arc with the IP identifying the navigation source and talking through the cross-check between the bearing pointer and the DME readout. This is SP's first exposure to cross-checking the bearing pointer against the DME readout at the same rate, and keeping both in the scan together has not yet been built. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to begin keeping the bearing pointer in the cross-check independently alongside the DME readout, with the IP available to confirm the source.
texts_at.1: SP used the radio aids to hold orientation on the arc to the standard expected at this stage, drifting to 2 DME off the arc, at the tolerance limit, before the cross-check caught it. The correction followed IP directing a check of the navigation source rather than SP's own cross-check. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to keep the bearing pointer in the cross-check alongside the DME readout, not only when a deviation is already visible.
texts_at.2: SP resumed a full cross-check on its own initiative during the intercept, drifting around 1.5 DME off the arc before correcting back onto the arc without IP intervention. The scan is still dwelling on the DME readout for a period before the bearing pointer is brought back in. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to keep the bearing pointer and the DME readout in the scan together, not resume one after the other.
texts_at.3: SP verified the navigation aid setup before the intercept and maintained a continuous cross-check between the bearing pointer, the DME readout and the flight instruments on most of the arc, holding it within 1 DME. One short stretch showed a narrower scan during a busy segment of the intercept, without a deviation resulting. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to hold the same scan width through that busy segment as through the rest of the arc.

texts_above.1: SP used the radio aids to hold orientation on the arc, drifting to about 2 DME off the arc, at the tolerance limit, before the cross-check caught it. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP resumed a full cross-check on its own initiative during the intercept, drifting about 1.5 DME off the arc before correcting back onto the arc without IP intervention. Keeping the bearing pointer and the DME readout in the scan together, rather than resuming one after the other, would remove that drift. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady cross-check discipline.
texts_above.3: SP verified the navigation aid setup before the intercept and maintained a continuous cross-check between the bearing pointer, the DME readout and the flight instruments, keeping orientation relative to the station at all times and holding the arc within 1 DME. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed scan integration.
texts_above.4: SP checked and identified the navigation source before the intercept and kept an even, uninterrupted cross-check throughout the arc, reporting aircraft position relative to the station accurately at any moment and holding the arc within about 0.3 DME. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior orientation awareness.

error_modes.label: Wind correction while established on the arc
error_modes.source: general:null (Basic A/C Control Criteria apply) | conditions:same as Course Intercepts

texts.0: SP, due to flying nominal arc headings without any allowance for the known wind, did not compensate for drift while established on the arc. The aircraft was pushed steadily off the published distance and the deviation grew beyond 2 DME with no correction applied. IP had to intervene and set the drift correction required to hold the arc.
texts.1: SP, due to applying a wind correction only after the deviation was visible on the DME readout, did not prevent the drift off the arc. The distance from the arc reached 2 DME, at the tolerance limit, and a correction was applied only after IP verbally identified the wind effect. The same drift reappeared as soon as the aircraft turned into the downwind portion of the arc.
texts.2: SP, due to a wind correction that was not updated as the arc heading changed, did not hold the published distance exactly. The aircraft drifted about 1.5 DME off the arc, between the 1 DME and 2 DME limits. SP noticed the trend, adjusted the correction turn and returned to the arc without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP allowed for the wind while established on the arc, adjusting the drift correction as the arc heading changed, and held the distance from the arc within 1 DME. Corrections were anticipated rather than reactive.
texts.4: SP anticipated the wind effect around the whole arc and continuously updated the drift correction, holding the distance from the arc within about 0.3 DME. The DME readout showed no sustained drift in any sector of the arc.
texts.marginal: SP held the arc within tolerance, but the drift correction was updated only after the DME had moved about 0.9 DME toward the outside of the arc in the downwind sector. The correction was adequate but always applied after the drift had developed. SP is expected to update the wind correction as the arc heading changes so that the drift does not build before it is countered.

texts_at.0: SP flew the arc with the IP setting the drift correction needed for the wind and talking through the DME trend as the arc heading changed. This is SP's first exposure to updating a wind correction as the arc heading changes, and recognizing the repeating DME trend that calls for it has not yet been built. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to begin recognizing the DME trend independently as the cue for a wind correction, with the IP available to confirm the amount.
texts_at.1: SP compensated for wind on the arc to the standard expected at this stage, drifting to 2 DME off the arc, at the tolerance limit, before the correction was applied. The correction followed IP identifying the wind effect verbally rather than SP's own recognition of the drift. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to look for a repeating DME trend as the cue for a wind correction rather than waiting for it to reach the tolerance.
texts_at.2: SP noticed the trend and adjusted the correction turn without prompting, drifting about 1.5 DME off the arc before returning to the arc without IP intervention. The correction is still updated after the arc heading has already changed rather than as it changes. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to update the drift correction as the arc heading changes rather than after the drift has become visible.
texts_at.3: SP allowed for the wind while established on the arc, adjusting the drift correction as the arc heading changed, and held the distance from the arc within 1 DME around most of the arc. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to anticipate that downwind sector as reliably as the rest of the arc.

texts_above.2: SP noticed the trend and adjusted the correction turn without prompting, drifting about 1.5 DME off the arc before returning to the arc without IP intervention. texts_above.3: SP allowed for the wind while established on the arc, adjusting the drift correction as the arc heading changed and holding the distance from the arc within 1 DME, with corrections anticipated rather than reactive. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to faultless wind-drift management.

error_modes.label: Aircraft handling smoothness and trim
error_modes.source: general:null (Basic A/C Control Criteria apply) | xref:instrument-04:a,c

texts.0: SP, due to flying the arc with continuous out-of-trim control inputs and abrupt corrections, did not handle the aircraft with comfort and ease. Pitch and bank inputs were large and reversed frequently, and the resulting excursions took the aircraft more than 2 DME off the arc and more than 300 feet off the assigned altitude. IP had to intervene and stabilize the aircraft.
texts.1: SP, due to leaving the aircraft out of trim after each power change, did not control pitch and bank smoothly on the arc. Control forces were fought manually and the resulting oscillations reached 300 feet in altitude, at the tolerance limit, before SP retrimmed following IP verbal instruction. The workload created by the out-of-trim condition degraded the rest of the intercept.
texts.2: SP, due to trimming late after the roll-in on the intercept turn, did not fly the arc as smoothly as required. Small pitch oscillations produced altitude excursions of about 200 feet, between the 150 foot and 300 foot limits. SP retrimmed on its own initiative and the aircraft was stabilized without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP handled the aircraft with comfort and ease, trimming aileron, elevator and rudder after each configuration and power change. Control inputs were smooth and the aircraft remained within 1 DME of the arc and within 150 feet of the assigned altitude.
texts.4: SP flew the entire arc intercept trimmed and hands-light, with control inputs so small that altitude excursions stayed near 40 feet and the DME readout near 0.3 DME. Switch and power handling was flawless and did not disturb the aircraft attitude.
texts.marginal: SP kept all parameters within tolerance, but the aircraft was flown slightly out of trim in pitch for most of the arc, which required continuous manual pressure and produced small repetitive altitude corrections. Trim was reset only when the deviation became noticeable. SP is expected to retrim immediately after each power change so that the aircraft can be held on parameters with minimal control force.

texts_at.0: SP flew the arc with the IP calling the out-of-trim condition and talking through the retrim needed after each power change. This is SP's first exposure to trimming immediately after a power change on a DME arc, and the habit of retrimming rather than holding pressure has not yet been built. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to begin retrimming independently after each power change, with the IP available to call any residual pressure.
texts_at.1: SP handled the aircraft while flying the arc to the standard expected at this stage, with oscillations reaching 300 feet in altitude and the arc distance opening to 2 DME, both at the tolerance limit, before the aircraft was retrimmed. SP is expected to trim immediately after each power change rather than fighting the resulting control forces manually.
texts_at.2: SP retrimmed on its own initiative during the intercept, producing altitude excursions of about 200 feet and letting the arc distance drift to about 1.5 DME before the aircraft was stabilized without IP intervention. The trim is still reset a moment after the roll-in on the intercept turn rather than with it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to retrim as the roll-in is made rather than after the residual pressure is felt.
texts_at.3: SP handled the aircraft with comfort and ease, trimming aileron, elevator and rudder after each configuration and power change, on most of the arc, remaining within 1 DME of the arc and within 150 feet of the assigned altitude. One segment needed a slightly larger control input following a closely spaced pair of corrections, without leaving the standard. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to keep the same smoothness through closely spaced corrections as through widely spaced ones.

texts_above.1: SP handled the aircraft while flying the arc, with oscillations reaching about 300 feet in altitude, at the tolerance limit, before the aircraft was retrimmed. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP retrimmed on its own initiative during the intercept, producing altitude excursions of about 200 feet before the aircraft was stabilized without IP intervention. Retrimming as the roll-in is made, rather than a moment after it, would keep those excursions smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid trim discipline.
texts_above.3: SP handled the aircraft with comfort and ease, trimming aileron, elevator and rudder after each configuration and power change, with control inputs smooth and the aircraft remaining within 1 DME of the arc and within 150 feet of the assigned altitude. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed aircraft handling.

error_modes.label: Task prioritization and workload management during the intercept
error_modes.source: general:null (Basic A/C Control Criteria apply) | conditions:same as Course Intercepts

texts.0: SP, due to poor workload management that left the navigation problem unsolved until the arc was already approaching, did not sequence the intercept tasks correctly. Aircraft control was released while SP worked the DME and bearing problem, and the aircraft passed more than 2 DME through the arc with the altitude uncontrolled. IP had to intervene, fly the aircraft and re-establish it on the arc.
texts.1: SP, due to attempting the navigation computation and a radio call at the same time as the intercept turn, did not prioritize aircraft control. The distance from the arc reached 2 DME, at the tolerance limit, while SP was heads-down, and the correction was made only after IP verbally reordered the tasks. The intercept was completed late and with continuous prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to a task sequence that placed the navigation setup after the turn had started, did not manage the workload of the intercept efficiently. The delay allowed the aircraft to drift about 1.5 DME off the arc, between the 1 DME and 2 DME limits. SP reprioritized to flying the aircraft first, then completed the setup and regained the arc without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP sequenced the intercept tasks correctly, completing the navigation setup and the lead computation before the turn onto the arc. Aircraft control was retained as the priority throughout and the arc was held within 1 DME with no other parameter exceeding its tolerance.
texts.4: SP planned the arc intercept well ahead, distributing the navigation, radio and flying tasks so that no phase was rushed. Every task was completed at the appropriate moment, the arc was held within about 0.3 DME and SP retained spare capacity to answer IP questions during the intercept.
texts.marginal: SP completed all intercept tasks within tolerance, but the navigation setup and the lead computation were consistently finished only just before the turn, leaving no margin for an unexpected clearance change. Radio calls were answered at the expense of a brief interruption in the scan. SP is expected to complete the intercept preparation earlier so that spare capacity remains available during the turn onto the arc.

texts_at.0: SP flew the intercept with the IP sequencing the navigation setup, the radio calls and the flying tasks and talking through the priority of each. This is SP's first exposure to sequencing the tasks of an arc intercept, and keeping aircraft control as the first priority has not yet been built. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to begin prioritizing aircraft control independently over the navigation computation and the radio call, with the IP available to confirm the sequence.
texts_at.1: SP managed the workload of the intercept to the standard expected at this stage, letting the distance from the arc reach 2 DME, at the tolerance limit, while heads-down on the navigation problem. The reordering of tasks followed IP's verbal direction rather than SP's own prioritization. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to prioritize aircraft control over the navigation computation and the radio call when they compete for the same moment.
texts_at.2: SP reprioritized to flying the aircraft first without prompting, drifting some 1.5 DME off the arc before completing the setup and regaining the arc. The navigation setup is still started after the turn onto the arc has begun rather than before it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to complete the navigation setup before the turn begins, not while it is already under way.
texts_at.3: SP sequenced the intercept tasks correctly, completing the navigation setup and the lead computation before the turn onto the arc on most intercepts, holding the arc within 1 DME with no other parameter exceeding tolerance. One intercept needed the setup finished right at the start of the turn rather than clearly before it, without a deviation resulting. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to build the same margin into that intercept as into the others.

texts_above.1: SP managed the workload of the intercept, letting the distance from the arc reach about 2 DME, at the tolerance limit, while heads-down on the navigation problem. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP reprioritized to flying the aircraft first without prompting, drifting about 1.5 DME off the arc before completing the setup and regaining the arc. Completing the navigation setup before the turn begins, rather than while it is already under way, would remove that drift. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady task prioritization.
texts_above.3: SP sequenced the intercept tasks correctly, completing the navigation setup and the lead computation before the turn onto the arc, retaining aircraft control as the priority throughout and holding the arc within 1 DME with no other parameter exceeding tolerance. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed workload sequencing.
texts_above.4: SP planned the arc intercept well ahead, distributing the navigation, radio and flying tasks so no phase was rushed, holding the arc within about 0.3 DME while retaining spare capacity to answer IP questions during the intercept. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior task management.

error_modes.label: LEAD POINT NOT REDUCED FOR AN INTERCEPT TURN OF LESS THAN 90 DEGREES

texts.0: SP, due to applying the full lead point computed for a 90 degree turn at 30 degrees of bank to an intercept turn of only 45 degrees, did not reduce it to one third as the technique requires. The turn onto the arc was started far too early and the aircraft rolled out more than 2 DME inside the arc with the DME still decreasing. IP had to intervene and direct the turn back out to the published arc distance.
texts.1: SP, due to using the whole calculated lead point on a 60 degree intercept turn instead of one half of it, did not place the roll-out on the published arc. The aircraft finished 2 DME inside the arc, at the tolerance limit, and was turned back out only after repeated verbal instruction from IP. The same unreduced lead point was used again on the following intercept.
texts.2: SP, due to only a partial reduction of the lead point for a turn of less than 90 degrees, did not roll out exactly on the published arc. The aircraft passed about 1.5 DME inside the arc, between the 1 DME and 2 DME limits, before the trend was stopped. SP saw the DME trend, corrected outward and re-established the arc in time without IP input.
texts.3: SP reduced the calculated lead point according to the amount of turn, using one half for a 60 degree turn, one third for 45 degrees and one sixth for 30 degrees, and rolled out on the published arc within 1 DME. The reduction was applied before the turn was started, so no re-intercept was required.
texts.4: SP scaled the lead point to the actual amount of turn on every intercept and rolled out on the published arc with deviations no greater than about 0.3 DME. Each intercept was flown as a single continuous turn, with the DME stopping on the nominal arc distance.
texts.marginal: SP stayed within the required tolerance, but the reduction of the lead point for turns of less than 90 degrees was estimated by feel instead of the fractions given by the technique. Every roll-out therefore finished about 0.9 DME inside the arc and needed a small outward correction. SP is expected to apply the standard one half, one third and one sixth reductions for 60, 45 and 30 degree turns so that the roll-out arrives on the arc.

texts_at.0: SP turned onto the arc with the IP talking through the reduction of the lead point for a turn of less than the full amount. This is SP's first exposure to reducing a computed lead point by fractions of the turn actually flown, and applying the correct fraction has not yet been built. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to begin reducing the lead point independently by the standard fractions, with the IP available to confirm the amount.
texts_at.1: SP reduced the lead point to the standard expected at this stage, rolling out 2 DME inside the arc, at the tolerance limit, before turning back out. The correction followed repeated verbal instruction from IP rather than SP's own reduction of the lead. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to apply the standard fractions for turns of less than 90 degrees before the turn is started, not after the roll-out shows the arc has been missed.
texts_at.2: SP saw the DME trend without prompting, corrected outward and re-established the arc in time, passing about 1.5 DME inside the arc. The reduction of the lead point is still only partial for turns of less than 90 degrees. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to apply the full one-half, one-third or one-sixth reduction rather than a partial one.
texts_at.3: SP reduced the calculated lead point according to the amount of turn on most intercepts, using one half for a 60 degree turn, one third for 45 degrees and one sixth for 30 degrees, rolling out on the published arc within 1 DME. One intercept needed a small outward correction after a slightly optimistic reduction, without leaving the standard. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to apply that fraction as precisely on the smaller turns as on the larger ones.

texts_above.1: SP reduced the lead point, rolling out about 2 DME inside the arc, at the tolerance limit, before turning back out. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP saw the DME trend without prompting, corrected outward and re-established the arc in time, passing about 1.5 DME inside the arc. Applying the full fractional reduction rather than a partial one would remove that pass-through. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid lead-point reduction.
texts_above.3: SP reduced the calculated lead point according to the amount of turn, using one half for a 60 degree turn, one third for 45 degrees and one sixth for 30 degrees, and rolled out on the published arc within 1 DME with the reduction applied before the turn was started. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed fractional computation.
texts_above.4: SP scaled the lead point to the actual amount of turn on every intercept and rolled out on the published arc with deviations no greater than about 0.3 DME, flying each intercept as a single continuous turn. error_modes.label: NO-WIND TURN RADIUS USED AS THE LEAD POINT WITH NO ALLOWANCE FOR THE WIND

texts.0: SP, due to taking the calculated turn radius as the lead point without recognizing that the formula gives a no-wind value, did not allow for the tailwind component in the intercept turn. Groundspeed through the turn was well above the value used in the computation, the actual radius was much larger and the aircraft went more than 2 DME through the arc with the deviation still increasing. IP had to intervene and set the turn required to regain the published arc.
texts.1: SP, due to using the no-wind turn radius unchanged as the lead point, did not increase it for the wind component along the intercept. The aircraft rolled out 2 DME outside the arc, at the tolerance limit, and closed back onto the arc only after IP verbally directed the correction. The same unadjusted lead point was carried into the next intercept.
texts.2: SP, due to a lead point corrected for the wind only after the turn had been started, did not roll out on the published arc distance. The aircraft finished about 1.5 DME outside the arc, between the 1 DME and 2 DME limits. SP recognized the overshoot on the DME readout, tightened the turn and returned to the arc without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP treated the calculated turn radius as a no-wind lead point and adjusted it for the wind component before starting the intercept turn, rolling out on the published arc within 1 DME. The adjustment was made in the direction of the actual groundspeed through the turn.
texts.4: SP corrected the computed turn radius for the wind on every intercept and rolled out on the published arc with deviations of about 0.3 DME at most. The arc was captured in a single turn, with no follow-up correction needed after roll-out.
texts.marginal: SP held the arc inside the required tolerance, but the no-wind turn radius was used as the lead point on all intercepts regardless of the wind. On the downwind intercepts each roll-out finished about 0.9 DME outside the arc and had to be closed with an extra turn. SP is expected to correct the computed turn radius for the wind so that the roll-out arrives on the arc.

texts_at.0: SP turned onto the arc with the IP talking through the no-wind turn radius and the adjustment it needs for the wind component. This is SP's first exposure to recognizing that the turn radius formula gives a no-wind value, and adjusting it for the actual wind has not yet been built. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to begin adjusting the turn radius independently for the wind component, with the IP available to confirm the correction.
texts_at.1: SP allowed for the wind in the turn radius to the standard expected at this stage, rolling out 2 DME outside the arc, at the tolerance limit, before closing back onto the arc. The correction followed IP's verbal direction rather than SP's own recomputation of the lead. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to increase the no-wind turn radius for the wind component along the intercept rather than leaving it unadjusted.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the overshoot on the DME readout without prompting, tightening the turn and returning to the arc, finishing about 1.5 DME outside the arc. The wind correction is still applied after the turn has been started rather than before it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to correct the turn radius for the wind before the turn is started, not once it is already under way.
texts_at.3: SP treated the calculated turn radius as a no-wind lead point and adjusted it for the wind component before starting the intercept turn on most intercepts, rolling out on the published arc within 1 DME. SP is expected to make that adjustment before the turn on every intercept, not only most of them.

error_modes.label: RADIALS PER NM NOT RECOMPUTED FOR THE ARC ACTUALLY FLOWN (60 DIVIDED BY ARC)

texts.0: SP, due to reusing the six radials of lead learned on a 20 NM arc while flying a 10 NM arc, did not recompute the radials per NM with 60 divided by the arc distance, which gives 6 radials per NM on a 10 NM arc. The turn off the arc was therefore started with half the lead required and the aircraft flew through the desired radial by more than 10 degrees with no correction started. IP had to intervene and assign the heading to re-intercept the radial.
texts.1: SP, due to carrying a lead in radials over from a previous arc, did not convert the turn radius into radials for the arc being flown. The turn off the arc was begun late and the roll-out finished 10 degrees off the desired radial, at the tolerance limit, and the course was re-established only after IP verbally provided the intercept heading.
texts.2: SP, due to an approximate figure for radials per NM instead of the 60 divided by arc computation, started the turn off the arc slightly late. The aircraft crossed about 8 degrees through the desired radial, between the 5 degree and 10 degree limits. SP recognized the overshoot on the CDI and re-intercepted the radial promptly without IP input.
texts.3: SP converted the turn radius into radials with the 60 divided by arc rule for the arc actually flown and rolled out on the desired radial within 5 degrees. The lead in radials was recomputed whenever the arc distance changed.
texts.4: SP computed the radials per NM for the arc being flown and started the turn off the arc at exactly that radial, rolling out on the desired course within about 2 degrees. No re-intercept of the radial was required.
texts.marginal: SP rolled out on the desired radial inside tolerance, but the lead in radials was carried over from the previous arc and only trimmed by feel, so each turn off the arc finished about 4-5 degrees through the course. The course was recovered every time, yet the same pattern repeated. SP is expected to recompute 60 divided by the arc distance for each arc so that the turn off the arc is started at the correct radial.

texts_at.0: SP flew the radial intercept with the IP computing the radials per NM for the arc actually being flown and talking through the lead needed. This is SP's first exposure to recomputing the lead in radials for the arc distance actually flown, and the arithmetic has not yet become routine. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to begin recomputing the radials-per-mile figure independently for each arc distance, with the IP available to confirm the value.
texts_at.1: SP recomputed radials per NM to the standard expected at this stage, crossing the desired radial by 10 degrees, at the tolerance limit, before the course was re-established. The correction followed IP verbally providing the intercept heading rather than SP's own recomputation. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to divide 60 by the arc distance actually being flown before every turn off the arc, not carry a figure from a previous arc.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the overshoot on the CDI without prompting, crossing about 8 degrees through the desired radial before re-intercepting it promptly. The radials-per-NM figure used is still an approximation rather than the 60 divided by arc computation. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to compute the figure exactly rather than estimating it, particularly on the less common arc distances.
texts_at.3: SP converted the turn radius into radials with the 60 divided by arc rule for the arc actually flown and rolled out on the desired radial within 5 degrees on most intercepts, recomputing the lead in radials whenever the arc distance changed. One intercept needed a small extra correction following a change of arc distance, without leaving the standard. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. error_modes.label: OFF-THE-WALL CDI READ AS DISTANCE STILL TO GO DURING THE RADIAL INTERCEPT

texts.0: SP, due to waiting for the CDI to come off full deflection before turning, did not accept that at normal T-6 airspeeds the needle stays off the wall within 10 degrees of the desired course throughout the intercept. The turn was started only when the needle began to center, long past the small lead point required, and the aircraft flew through the course by more than 10 degrees with the deviation still growing. IP had to intervene and assign the re-intercept heading.
texts.1: SP, due to reading the off the wall CDI as if the course were still far ahead, did not start the intercept turn at the computed lead point. The roll-out finished 10 degrees off the desired course, at the tolerance limit, and the course was regained only after repeated verbal instruction from IP.
texts.2: SP, due to a late interpretation of the off the wall CDI presentation, started the intercept turn shortly after the lead point had passed. The aircraft crossed about 8 degrees through the desired course, between the 5 degree and 10 degree limits. SP read the needle rate, stopped the overshoot and settled on course in time without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP interpreted the CDI as an off the wall indication within 10 degrees of the desired course and used it together with the computed lead point, rolling out on course within 5 degrees. The needle was watched from the beginning of the intercept rather than after it had started to move.
texts.4: SP used the off the wall CDI presentation correctly throughout the intercept and rolled out on the desired course within about 2 degrees. The small lead point required at normal T-6 airspeeds was applied exactly, so the needle centered as the wings came level.
texts.marginal: SP rolled out on course inside tolerance, but every intercept turn was started once the CDI had visibly begun to move rather than at the computed lead point, because the off the wall needle was read as spare distance. Each roll-out finished about 4-5 degrees off course and required a further correction. SP is expected to treat the CDI as off the wall from the start of the intercept and turn at the computed lead point.

texts_at.0: SP flew the radial intercept with the IP reading the off-the-wall CDI presentation and talking through the computed lead point for the turn. This is SP's first exposure to reading an off-the-wall CDI as a small remaining lead rather than as distance still to go, and starting the turn from it has not yet been built. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to begin reading the off-the-wall CDI independently from the start of the intercept, with the IP available to confirm the lead point.
texts_at.1: SP read the off-the-wall CDI to the standard expected at this stage, crossing the desired course by 10 degrees, at the tolerance limit, before the course was regained. SP is expected to treat the CDI as off-the-wall from the start of the intercept rather than waiting for it to begin moving before turning.
texts_at.2: SP read the needle rate without prompting, stopping the overshoot and settling on course in time, crossing about 8 degrees through the desired course. The intercept turn is still started once the needle has begun visibly moving rather than at the computed lead point. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to start the turn at the computed lead point rather than waiting for a visible needle movement.
texts_at.3: SP interpreted the CDI as an off-the-wall indication within 10 degrees of the desired course and used it together with the computed lead point on most intercepts, rolling out on course within 5 degrees. SP is expected to start that intercept at the lead point as precisely as the others.

texts_above.2: SP read the needle rate without prompting, stopping the overshoot and settling on course in time, crossing about 8 degrees through the desired course. Starting the turn at the computed lead point, rather than waiting for a visible needle movement, would remove that overshoot. texts_above.3: SP interpreted the CDI as an off-the-wall indication within 10 degrees of the desired course and used it together with the computed lead point, rolling out on course within 5 degrees with the needle watched from the beginning of the intercept. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed presentation reading.
texts_above.4: SP used the off-the-wall CDI presentation correctly throughout the intercept and rolled out on the desired course within about 2 degrees, applying the small lead point required at normal T-6 airspeeds exactly so the needle centered as the wings came level. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional lead-point timing.

error_modes.label: ALTITUDE RESTRICTION AT THE ARC OR RADIAL INTERSECTION NOT APPLIED

texts.0: SP, due to lack of knowledge of the rules for altitude restrictions at arc and radial intersections, did not hold the assigned altitude until the intersection defining the step down was crossed. The descent was started while still established on the arc and the aircraft was more than 300 feet below the restriction before the fix, still descending. IP had to intervene and stop the descent to restore the required altitude.
texts.1: SP, due to accepting the clearance without checking where the altitude restriction at the arc and radial intersection applied, did not delay the descent until the fix. The aircraft was 300 feet below the restriction altitude before the intersection, at the tolerance limit, and leveled off only after IP verbally called the restriction.
texts.2: SP, due to a late review of the altitude restriction at the intersection of the arc and the radial, started the descent slightly before the fix. The aircraft was about 200 feet below the restriction altitude, between the 150 foot and 300 foot limits, as the intersection was crossed. SP recognized the error, arrested the descent and returned to the required altitude without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP identified the altitude restriction applying at the arc and radial intersection and held the assigned altitude within 150 feet until the intersection was crossed. The descent was started only once the restriction no longer applied.
texts.4: SP had the altitude restriction at the arc and radial intersection established before the intercept and crossed the fix at the required altitude with deviations no greater than about 40 feet. The descent was initiated at the intersection itself, with no anticipation.
texts.marginal: SP respected the altitude restriction at the arc and radial intersection, but the descent was started just before the fix on each intercept, leaving the aircraft 130-150 feet low as the intersection was crossed. The restriction was met every time, yet the same anticipation repeated. SP is expected to hold the assigned altitude until the intersection is actually crossed.

texts_at.0: SP flew the arc and radial intersection with the IP calling the altitude restriction and talking through where it applied before the descent. This is SP's first exposure to holding altitude until an intersection restriction is actually crossed, and checking where the restriction applies has not yet been built. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to begin checking the altitude restriction independently before starting the descent, with the IP available to confirm where it applies.
texts_at.1: SP applied the altitude restriction at the intersection to the standard expected at this stage, reaching 300 feet below the restriction altitude, at the tolerance limit, before leveling off. The level-off followed IP's verbal call of the restriction rather than SP's own review of the clearance. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to check where an altitude restriction applies before starting the descent, not after the aircraft is already below it.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the error and arrested the descent without prompting, reaching about 200 feet below the restriction altitude before returning to the required altitude. The review of the restriction is still made a moment before the fix rather than well before it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to review the restriction earlier in the intercept so the descent is not started before it can be respected.
texts_at.3: SP identified the altitude restriction applying at the arc and radial intersection and held the assigned altitude within 150 feet until the intersection was crossed on most intercepts, starting the descent only once the restriction no longer applied. One intercept needed a slightly later review of the restriction, without a deviation resulting. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to review that restriction as early as on the other intercepts.

texts_above.1: SP applied the altitude restriction at the intersection, reaching about 300 feet below the restriction altitude, at the tolerance limit, before leveling off. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the error and arrested the descent without prompting, reaching about 200 feet below the restriction altitude before returning to the required altitude. Reviewing the restriction earlier in the intercept, rather than a moment before the fix, would remove that excursion. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent restriction awareness.
texts_above.3: SP identified the altitude restriction applying at the arc and radial intersection and held the assigned altitude within 150 feet until the intersection was crossed, starting the descent only once the restriction no longer applied. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined restriction management.
texts_above.4: SP had the altitude restriction at the arc and radial intersection established before the intercept and crossed the fix at the required altitude with deviations no greater than about 40 feet, initiating the descent at the intersection itself with no anticipation needed. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to faultless restriction planning.
